title: Deployments as Controlled Experiments
html:
Deployments as Controlled Experiments

The limits introduced in Chapter 9 depend on how much work the running code performs. A new version can use more database time for the same result, invalidating those limits without producing a functional error. That possibility makes performance evidence part of a release decision, alongside correctness and startup checks.

The Recommendation Service team had rewritten a database query. The new query returned the same recommendations as the old one, and in an isolated benchmark it ran faster, so the team released it the usual way, through a rolling update that replaced instances one at a time. As the new instances began serving production traffic, database connection occupancy rose. A lookup that had held a connection for an average of 70 milliseconds now held it for about 85, requests began waiting for connections, and product-page response times grew, even though customers continued to receive valid recommendations. Rolling back to the previous version brought connection occupancy and wait times back to normal.

In the review, the engineers asked why the benchmark had missed the regression and why the rollout kept going after connection occupancy rose. The benchmark had run the query against a copy of production data one request at a time, which is the condition under which the new query was faster. In production, hundreds of lookups ran concurrently against the same database, and under that contention the new query plan lost its advantage. The rollout continued because the deployment controller checked only that each new instance started and passed its readiness check. Nothing in the release compared resource use between the two versions before the next instance was replaced.

Chapter 6 covered how to package and run a reproducible artifact. In this chapter, we build the release process that would have stopped this rollout after the first instance: a written hypothesis about what the change should do, a canary that receives representative traffic, evaluation gates derived from measured variation, and a restoration procedure tested before it is needed. We also look at the releases that are hardest to undo, those that change stored data or interfaces that other teams depend on.

The Release Hypothesis

A release plan begins with two statements: the improvement the change is expected to deliver, and the production condition most likely to prove that expectation wrong. For the recommendation query, the expected improvement was less database work for the same results, and the main uncertainty was whether that improvement would hold under concurrent requests against production data. Writing both down before the release gives the team a reference point. When a measurement changes during the rollout, engineers compare it with the stated expectation to decide whether it should stop the rollout or falls within ordinary variation.

The uncertainty also determines what to measure. A question about database work under concurrency calls for connection occupancy, connection acquisition time, query execution time, recommendation delivery, and product-page response time. CPU utilization, the measure most dashboards show first, would reveal little about pressure on the connection pool.

Each Recommendation Service instance has a pool of 40 connections and handles about 400 lookups per second. The number of connections in use at any moment equals the lookup rate multiplied by how long each lookup holds its connection, so at 400 lookups per second and 70 milliseconds per lookup, an instance keeps about 28 connections busy on average. Table \(\ref{tab:release-connection-demand}\) shows how the new query changed that figure.

The new query increased mean occupancy from 28 to 34 of the 40 connections, halving the average unassigned capacity from 12 to 6. Lookups do not arrive evenly, so the pool needs headroom above its average use to absorb bursts, and the closer average use comes to the pool size, the more often a burst exceeds it and requests start to wait. During bursts, fewer unassigned connections were available, so acquisition waits increased by more than the 15-millisecond increase in mean connection occupancy alone might suggest. The table cannot predict the resulting latency percentiles, but it shows why the engineers needed acquisition measurements before exposing more traffic to the new version. Finding the cause was a separate task. The team reproduced the slowdown by running the query concurrently with representative parameters, which pointed to an index choice that performed well in isolation and poorly under contention.

Other releases call for other hypotheses, about memory allocation, backend calls per request, event volume, or response correctness. In each case, the plan names the observation the team expects and the regression that would stop the rollout.

Deployment and Exposure

Installing new code and exposing customers to it are separate steps, and keeping them separate gives the team more control. A team can install a binary with the new query path disabled, verify that it starts and remains compatible, and then enable the path for selected requests. Alternatively, the router can send a fraction of requests to instances that run the new binary. These choices determine what the team can reverse and how much work the change can affect before anyone detects a problem, and Table \(\ref{tab:deploy-strategies}\) summarizes the common mechanisms.

These mechanisms can be combined, so that a blue-green setup can send a weighted share of traffic to the new environment as a canary before the full switch, a rolling update can pause between steps for evaluation, and a feature flag can restrict new behavior further inside the new version. The right combination depends on what the release is testing. A query regression needs representative database work, a new response format needs every consumer to be compatible with it, and a memory leak needs an observation period that lets retained memory accumulate to a measurable level.

Rolling Updates

A rolling update suits services whose old and new instances can serve traffic side by side. The deployment controller starts replacement instances and removes old ones according to a policy such as the one in Listing \(\ref{lst:ch10-rolling}\), and Figure \(\ref{fig:ch10-rolling}\) steps through one replacement.

[
  caption={A rolling replacement policy with temporary extra capacity.},
  label={lst:ch10-rolling}
]
strategy:
  type: RollingUpdate
  rollingUpdate:
    maxSurge: 1
    maxUnavailable: 0

This policy lets the controller add one extra instance at a time and forbids it from deliberately taking an instance out of service before its replacement is ready. It cannot prevent instances from failing on their own, and it says nothing about whether the remaining instances have the throughput the traffic requires. It also hides a cost that matters for connection limits. An instance that is shutting down can keep its database connections open while its replacement starts, so the database has to accommodate every live process, including draining instances and any autoscaling overlap, rather than the number implied by the surge setting.

The readiness check that the controller relies on shows only that an instance is prepared to accept requests. A new instance can pass it and then run a far more expensive query once real traffic arrives, which is exactly what happened with the recommendation release. A plain rolling update therefore needs an additional release policy whenever promotion should depend on performance. Similarly, a deployment progress deadline reports a rollout that has stalled, but it does not roll anything back, so automatic restoration requires a controller or an operating procedure that takes that action.

Blue-Green Environments

Blue-green deployment keeps two complete environments, one serving customers, called blue, and one idle, called green. The team installs the new release in green, tests it there without any production traffic, and then switches the router so that new requests go to green, as Figure \(\ref{fig:ch10-bluegreen}\) shows. Because blue remains ready to serve, switching back is a routing change rather than an instance-by-instance replacement, which can make restoration much faster.

Several details limit that advantage. Connections and requests that started before the switch can continue on the new environment afterward, and an environment that has been idle may need warming before it can accept the full request rate. Both environments may also run connection pools, background workers, and scheduled tasks, so Baodium’s cutover plan covers those processes as well, because starting a second environment must not create a second active scheduler or double the background workload. Most important, the two environments usually share a database, and a new version that writes data the old version cannot read can make blue unusable even though its processes are healthy. We return to that problem later in the chapter.

::: fieldnote

**Cloudflare, July 2019**

Cloudflare’s postmortem attributes its July 2, 2019 outage to a new rule for its web application firewall. The rule contained a regular expression that could backtrack catastrophically, and on machines across the network it consumed so much processor time that customers received errors for 27 minutes. Firewall rules were deployed to the whole network within seconds, because emergency rules against new attacks need to take effect everywhere at once, and as a result an ordinary rule change bypassed the gradual rollout that most of Cloudflare’s software went through. Cloudflare restored traffic by disabling the managed firewall rules globally, then fixed the rule and re-enabled the firewall.

A rule that executes is code, and it needs a canary, a comparison against a concurrent baseline, and a way to stop it, in the same way that a binary does. The recovery also depended on a control that disabled the rules across the entire network, which existed before the incident and worked during it. Source: original published account.

:::

A Representative Canary

When the team re-released the corrected query, it used a canary, which limits the first exposure to a small share of production traffic while the team compares the new version with the stable one. Figure \(\ref{fig:ch10-canary}\) shows the decision the canary exists to support. A canary is only as useful as the traffic and resources it receives, however, and most of the work in designing one goes into making that traffic representative.

Suppose Recommendation Service runs 20 instances, each receiving about 400 lookups per second, for a fleet total of about 8,000. Routing five percent of requests to one canary instance gives it about 400 lookups per second, and the other 19 instances share the remaining 95 percent at about the same rate each. The canary therefore experiences the same per-instance load as the stable instances, which is the condition under which the original regression appeared.

The size of the canary is a trade-off between exposure and evidence. A small canary affects few customers but may collect too few requests for a stable estimate of a high percentile, while a larger canary collects evidence faster at the cost of exposing more customers. Five percent is a starting point, and the team supplements it with early signals, such as connection acquisition time, that respond to a regression well before a high percentile can be estimated reliably.

The routing weight and the number of canary instances must be chosen together. If the team spread the same five percent across five canary instances, each would receive only about 80 lookups per second, and at that rate the new query might show no acquisition delay at all, even though it would create contention at the normal rate of 400. The router therefore controls the traffic weight independently of instance count, and the release dashboard reports the rate each instance receives, because a configured percentage is only a request to the router, and the measured rate is what the comparison depends on.

Cohort Selection

Request rate is only one part of a fair comparison. Region, catalog size, query parameters, cache state, and customer behavior all affect resource use, so a canary that happens to serve mostly small catalogs can look faster than a stable population serving large ones. An internal-user cohort is useful for functional feedback but says little about production performance. For the query release, Baodium used a production cohort in which every relevant request class was represented, compared the known cost categories between the two populations, and inspected instances individually whenever fleet averages hid an imbalance.

Assigning each customer persistently to one version prevents a customer from switching between versions in the middle of an interaction, but it also means that five percent of customers may generate more or less than five percent of requests, so the release record includes both the assignment and the observed request volume. A single canary instance can also be affected by its node or placement. When its measurements look anomalous and the cause is unclear, the team repeats the comparison on another placement before blaming the query, and exposure does not increase while that investigation is open.

Startup and Warm State

A new instance opens connections, loads metadata, and fills its local caches as its first requests arrive, and those costs are part of the deployment’s behavior, so they need their own observation rather than being excluded from the result. If an instance cannot serve normal traffic until it has finished preparing, either its readiness check must wait for that preparation or the router must increase its traffic gradually. A fixed delay after startup helps only when testing has shown what happens during that delay, because five uneventful minutes may mean only that a rarely used path has not run yet and a large cache remains empty.

Shared Dependencies

Canary and stable instances usually share a database, and that creates the canary’s main blind spot. An expensive canary query can raise database CPU or contention to the point where both populations slow down, and when both slow down together, the gap between them shrinks, so a harmful change can look harmless. A small difference between canary and stable response times is therefore not evidence that a release is acceptable, because both may have deteriorated. Baodium compares the two versions and also checks absolute limits on customer-facing latency and shared resources. The traffic percentage limits how many requests reach the canary directly, but a shared dependency can spread the consequences to every request.

Shadow testing, in which copies of production reads are sent to the new version and the responses discarded, has the same property. The copied reads consume real backend capacity even though nobody uses their results, so shadow traffic needs its own allowance, and requests that change state must either run in isolation or have their effects suppressed, which in turn limits what the test can prove.

::: decision

**Promote or hold?**

Recommendation Service has 20 instances, each handling about 400 lookups per second. The canary is one instance at five percent exposure. After twenty minutes it shows page p99 at 231 ms against a baseline of 220 ms, no errors, and mean connection occupancy of 74 ms against a baseline of 70 ms. The release owner wants to go to 25 percent.

**Promote. An 11-millisecond difference at the p99 is within ordinary variation, and there are no errors.**

**Hold. The occupancy difference is small but consistent, and it is the measurement that scales with exposure.**

**Promote, but only to 10 percent, and re-evaluate.**

—

In twenty minutes, the canary handles about 400 lookups per second for 1,200 seconds, or 480,000 lookups, so with complete recording, about 4,800 of them fall in the slowest one percent. That is a substantial sample, but its duration, request mix, and the dependence between successive requests all affect the comparison, and neither the mean nor the p99 difference alone proves a regression.

The occupancy difference means \(400 \times 0.004 = 1.6\) more connections in use on the canary instance. If the same rate and difference held on all 20 instances, full promotion would add about 32 connections across the fleet, although shared-database contention could change those durations, so the estimate needs testing.

Under B, the team pauses promotion and compares the observations with the release gate written before the rollout, checking that the workloads match. If the measured difference falls within the accepted range, the gate permits promotion. C is reasonable only if the evaluation plan already calls for a bounded intermediate step with explicit stop criteria. A assumes the variation is acceptable without making that comparison.

:::

Evaluation Gates

A gate records, before the release begins, the evidence required before exposure increases. Writing it in advance matters because a team looking at a promising canary is inclined to explain away an inconvenient number, whereas a criterion recorded beforehand cannot be adjusted to fit the result.

For the recommendation change, connection occupancy was the most direct early measurement, and it had to be compared per version. At five percent exposure, a 15-millisecond increase on the canary raises the fleet-wide mean by only 0.75 milliseconds, assuming comparable requests and no secondary effects, which is easy to miss in a combined average. A version-specific comparison preserves the full 15 milliseconds. The gate also checks acquisition failures and the customer-facing page, so that an improved average cannot hide requests that failed or were never completed.

Each evaluation leads to one of three outcomes.

Promote.

The required evidence is present, comparable, and satisfies the recorded criteria.

Pause.

Exposure remains at its current level while the team resolves missing evidence, an insufficient sample, or an unexplained difference.

Abort.

New exposure to the candidate is removed through the tested restoration procedure.

A pause leaves the current canary population exposed, so it is the wrong response when that population is experiencing an unacceptable failure. In that case, the correct outcome is an abort.

A Sample Release Plan

Listing \(\ref{lst:ch10-release-plan}\) shows the level of detail that makes the query release reviewable. The values are specific to this case, and each one needs validation against ordinary variation and the product’s objectives.

[
  caption={An example release policy for the recommendation query.},
  label={lst:ch10-release-plan}
]
initial_exposure:
  traffic_percent: 5
  canary_instances: 1
  expected_lookups_per_instance_per_second: 400

evaluation:
  interval_minutes: 5
  minimum_canary_completions_per_interval: 50000
  passing_non_overlapping_intervals: 2

criteria:
  mean_connection_occupancy_delta_ms:
    maximum: 5

  connection_acquisition_p99_ms:
    maximum: 20

telemetry:
  missing_required_signal: pause
  maximum_blind_interval_seconds: 60
  after_blind_interval: restore_stable

promotion:
  next_stage_requires_recorded_pass: true

restoration:
  target: approved_stable_release

The sample requirement accompanies the elapsed interval because time alone guarantees nothing. At the expected rate, the canary completes about 120,000 lookups in five minutes, but the controller evaluates the measured count, so an interval in which the canary received too little traffic does not count as a pass. The occupancy margin of five milliseconds is far smaller than the original 15-millisecond regression, so that regression would fail this gate in the first interval, and the absolute limit on acquisition time prevents promotion when both versions are already experiencing serious pool contention.

Two further rules sit outside the performance criteria. Customer failures and incorrect data trigger an immediate abort, because the controller should not wait two five-minute intervals while requests are returning wrong results. The complete policy also names the person responsible for resolving a pause and a maximum duration for each stage, so that a canary waiting for a signal that never arrives does not run unattended indefinitely.

Deriving the Gate Values

The values in the policy are not defaults copied from another service. Each one comes from a short chain of reasoning that another team can repeat with its own measurements, starting from baseline variation and ending with the interval that produces the required sample.

Baseline variation.

Two weeks of stable data showed that one instance’s five-minute mean occupancy varied by about 1.5 milliseconds between intervals, mostly because the traffic mix changed, whereas sampling noise was much smaller. With a per-lookup standard deviation near 40 milliseconds, the standard error of a mean over 50,000 lookups is \(40/\sqrt{50{,}000}\), or about 0.2 milliseconds.

Smallest regression worth detecting.

From Table \(\ref{tab:release-connection-demand}\), one instance keeps about 28 connections busy at 400 lookups per second and 70 milliseconds, so each additional millisecond of mean occupancy adds about 0.4 connections. A five-millisecond increase raises average demand to 30 of 40, which the team judged the most it could accept before bursts regularly reached the pool limit, whereas the original 15-millisecond regression raised it to 34. The five-millisecond threshold is also about three times the ordinary interval-to-interval variation, so a healthy release rarely fails it by chance.

Minimum sample.

At 50,000 completions, sampling noise is negligible compared with the five-millisecond threshold, and the acquisition p99 rests on about 500 observations in the slowest percent. The same reasoning shows why gates on error rates need far more traffic. At a baseline error rate of 0.1 percent, 100 requests are expected to contain 0.1 errors and say nothing about whether the rate has doubled, and distinguishing 0.2 percent from 0.1 percent with useful confidence generally takes tens of thousands of requests in each version, depending on the comparison method.

Exposure while waiting.

At five percent, the canary received about 400 of the fleet’s 8,000 lookups per second, so two five-minute intervals exposed about 240,000 lookups to the candidate before the first promotion decision. The team accepted that exposure because the failure under test degraded page latency rather than correctness, and the immediate abort conditions already covered correctness.

Interval.

At the expected rate, five minutes yields about 120,000 lookups, more than twice the minimum, so a canary that receives only half its expected share qualifies. Requiring two nonoverlapping intervals guards against a single interval that coincides with an unusual swing in traffic.

A release with another kind of risk calls for its own chain of reasoning. A change expected to affect rare request classes needs a larger sample or a targeted test, and a change that could corrupt data needs a smaller initial exposure regardless of how long the sample then takes.

Observation Windows

The intervals in the release plan do not overlap for a specific reason. Two evaluations of a rolling five-minute window taken one minute apart share four minutes of observations, so treating them as two passes would count the same requests twice. Nonoverlapping intervals avoid that, although production measurements remain correlated from one interval to the next.

The size of a sample also depends on the event being measured. Hundreds of thousands of successful lookups give useful evidence about mean occupancy but say almost nothing about a failure that occurs once per million requests, which needs a targeted test or a broader observation plan. Some risks depend on elapsed time rather than request count, such as token refresh, scheduled work, cache expiration, and gradual memory growth, and those need observation periods that span them. The release owner chooses the interval to match the suspected failure and records which conditions the canary has not yet exercised.

Telemetry for the Decision

The release dashboard pairs each instance’s request rate with its connection occupancy, acquisition time, active connections, recommendation delivery, and page outcomes. Cohort percentiles are computed from the combined histogram observations rather than by averaging per-instance percentiles, for the reasons explained in Chapter 8. Attempted and refused requests are shown beside completed ones, because a version that rejects expensive work could otherwise look faster merely by leaving that work out of its completion times.

Each stage decision records the deployed artifact and configuration, the routing weight, the sample interval, the observed values, the thresholds, and the action taken. With that record, an engineer can later explain why exposure increased or why restoration began.

Promotion Beyond the First Stage

A clean result at five percent does not predict how the change will behave at full exposure, because the canary tests the new version only under its own share of traffic, and some costs grow with total exposure. A query can fit comfortably within the database’s CPU when one instance runs it and create contention when all 20 do, and a new cache namespace can generate more misses as each additional caller adopts it. Before treating a canary result as a capacity check, the team reviews the additional shared-resource demand expected at full exposure.

Baodium therefore advances through several stages while keeping the per-instance traffic representative. In the 20-instance fleet, a 15-percent stage assigns three instances to the candidate and 17 to the stable version, and each stage repeats the applicable checks, including the absolute database and customer measurements, because evidence from one stage applies only to its own level of exposure.

Restoration takes longer as the rollout advances. At the first stage, most instances already run the previous version, whereas near the end, restoring the old version may require starting or replacing most of the fleet, so the plan accounts for that time and for the load on the remaining instances while it happens. The final stage includes an observation period after full activation. With no stable cohort left for comparison, the evidence at that point comes from absolute limits, earlier comparisons, and per-request-class measurements.

Feature Flags

For the recommendation query, a feature flag could have separated installation from activation. Both query paths would ship in the same binary, and configuration would select a path for each request. The benefit is that turning the new path off becomes a configuration change rather than a deployment. The cost is an additional code path and an additional configuration state, so every flag needs an owner and a condition for its removal, and as the Knight Capital field note below shows, an obsolete activation path can cause a failure years after its original purpose has passed.

A deterministic assignment, computed from a stable identifier and a flag-specific salt, keeps each customer on the same variant throughout the release. The variant is evaluated once per operation and recorded with its telemetry, because version labels alone cannot distinguish the two paths when a single binary can execute both.

Disabling the flag stops new selections of the candidate path only after the change reaches every serving instance, so the restoration plan accounts for configuration-delivery delay, client-side caching of flag values, and the behavior when the flag service itself is unavailable. A default to the stable path is appropriate only while that path supports current data and configuration, and an application that keeps using the last flag value it retrieved may continue running the candidate path during a control-plane outage. That behavior must be understood before the flag is treated as an emergency control. After disabling the flag, the engineer confirms from telemetry which variant instances are executing, because writing the configuration and every instance applying it are separate events, and requests already in progress on the candidate path may complete after new selections have stopped.

A release flag is retired once validation and the restoration period are complete. A later deployment removes the old path, and the flag record is deleted once no deployed version depends on it. Operational switches that remain in place permanently need an owner and periodic testing of the fallback they control.

::: fieldnote

**Knight Capital, August 2012**

The SEC’s order against Knight Capital describes a deployment of new trading software to eight servers. The code was installed over several days, and a technician failed to copy it to one of the eight. No second person reviewed the deployment, and no written procedure required one. The new code reused a flag that had once activated an old, long-retired function called Power Peg, and that old code remained on the eighth server. When orders carrying the reused flag arrived on August 1, seven servers behaved correctly and the eighth began sending orders it should never have sent. The SEC reported more than four million executions in about 45 minutes and a loss exceeding $460 million.

During the incident, engineers removed the new code from the seven servers where it had been installed correctly. That made the situation worse, because orders with the flag then reached the old code on every server.

The incident connects to four points in this chapter. A deployment must be verified on every target, dead code should be removed rather than reactivated through a reused switch, rollback is a change in its own right and needs rehearsal, and a system needs a way to stop that does not depend on the code being stopped. Source: original published account.

:::

Rollback and Data Compatibility

The recommendation query could be rolled back freely because it did not change any stored data. Releases that do change stored data have a much narrower rollback window, because the old version must be able to read anything the new version has written. Suppose the catalog team wants to replace a category field with category_v2 to support a revised catalog feature. If new readers are deployed while some writers continue to update only category, those readers return outdated values, and if new writers are rolled back after updating only category_v2, the restored readers miss the new data. The way out is a staged compatibility release.

Expansion and Compatible Writers

Safe data changes follow an expand-then-contract order, which resembles replacing a road bridge. Engineers build the new bridge beside the old one, open it while the old bridge remains in service, divert traffic gradually, and close the old bridge only when nothing depends on it. In a schema change, the first release adds the new field while existing readers continue to use the old one. That schema change needs its own assessment of locking and resource use before it runs.

A compatibility release then writes both representations in the same database transaction. The deployment inventory includes background jobs, administrative tools, and recovery workers, because any of them may update the affected records, and before new readers are enabled, the team confirms that every active writer maintains both fields. The compatibility release becomes the approved rollback target for this period, and that choice matters. Rolling back to an earlier writer that updates only the old field would silently invalidate the new field for every process that has started reading it.

Backfill and Verification

Existing rows are converted in bounded batches whose rate is controlled separately from the application deployment, because the backfill competes with ordinary requests for database execution, locks, and I/O. Concurrent updates need a defined ordering rule, so that the backfill never overwrites a recently written value with an older copy of the source. The backfill can calculate the new value from the current row under appropriate transaction protection, or it can make each update conditional on the source version it read and retry on conflict.

Verification checks the relationship between the two representations. Counting non-null values in the new field shows that the values exist, not that they are current or correctly converted, so the check compares each converted value with its source. After verification, the team enables new readers progressively, and both representations continue to be maintained for the agreed rollback period.

Contraction

Stopping writes to the old field, or dropping it, ends compatibility with every version that depends on it, so that step happens in a separate release after the earlier rollback target has been retired. The check includes processes that run infrequently, because a monthly report or a recovery tool can depend on the old field long after the serving fleet has upgraded.

Dual writing also has a limit, because if the new representation permits values that the old one cannot express, writing both fields cannot make the change reversible, and rollback then requires an explicit restriction on new values, a conversion, or a plan to repair forward instead.

API and Event Compatibility

The same reasoning applies to interfaces, with one complication. Some consumers of an API are deployed by other teams or by customers on their own schedules, and the provider cannot upgrade them alongside its own release, so compatibility rules must cover clients that have not yet upgraded.

Adding a field to a response is compatible only with consumers that accept unknown fields. Renaming a field, adding an unexpected enum value, or changing the meaning of an existing value can break a consumer even though the HTTP status is unchanged. For a field replacement, the provider publishes both forms while consumers adopt the new one, contract tests verify the documented consumer requirements, and deployment data establishes which consumer versions remain active.

Events extend the overlap further, because an upgraded consumer may receive older events from a backlog, a retry queue, or a replay, and an older consumer restored during a rollback may receive events produced by the newer version. The compatibility policy therefore covers retained messages and recovery procedures as well as the versions currently serving requests, and Chapter 12 covers delivery and replay in detail.

Restoration as an Operating Procedure

A restoration test is meaningful only after the candidate has served requests and produced the kinds of state expected during the release. A rollback rehearsed on a fresh environment omits the case that fails in production, in which the new version has already written data that the old version has never read.

For the query change, the procedure begins with the release controller stopping promotion and redirecting new requests to the approved stable path. The application then drains or cancels candidate work according to each request’s contract, and engineers confirm which version is receiving requests and whether the resource measurements are recovering. An earlier image digest is only one part of that procedure, because the matching configuration, compatible credentials, routing policy, and sufficient serving capacity must all be available too.

Recovery does not always follow the routing change immediately. Database work already submitted can continue after the switch, and backlogs, lock contention, or cache entries left by the candidate can delay recovery, so when measurements fail to improve, the responder investigates those effects instead of repeating the rollback command. For a release that changes state, restoration also identifies accepted work that needs recovery or correction, because returning to the earlier binary does not undo events already emitted or external operations already performed. The release record therefore distinguishes the time taken to stop new candidate work from the time taken to restore customer service, because the two can differ substantially and each points to separate improvements.

Summary

The Recommendation Service query performed well in isolation and produced correct results, yet increased average connection occupancy from 70 to 85 milliseconds under production concurrency. During the rolling update, the deployment controller verified that new instances started successfully. It did not compare their resource use with the instances they replaced, so the regression spread until page latency increased.

A controlled release starts with a specific expectation and a measurement that could disprove it. The canary must receive a representative workload at the intended per-instance rate; comparing only global traffic can conceal a costly new version behind the unchanged majority. Later promotion stages repeat the checks because the effects of shared contention can change as more instances run the new code. Abort thresholds must account for ordinary metric variation while detecting changes large enough to threaten the resource budget.

Restoration is part of the release design. A previous image must remain compatible with the stored state, events, and APIs produced by the new version, and the rollback must be tested under realistic traffic. At Baodium, separate deployment pipelines did not always provide independent releases: teams still shared database tables and schema migrations. Chapter 11 examines that ownership problem and the costs of changing a service boundary.

::: hiddenassumptions

Assumption and scope & A query that returns correct results and improves an isolated benchmark also reduces resource use under production concurrency.
Condition that tests it & A new version increases connection occupancy or fails on a subset of instances.
Constraint or invariant & The canary instance receives about 400 lookups per second, the same rate as each stable instance, and promotion requires version-specific evidence measured against criteria recorded before the release.
Evidence and uncertainty & Mean connection occupancy rose from 70 to 85 milliseconds, raising average use from 28 to 34 of 40 connections per instance. Request mix, placement, cache state, and shared database contention can affect the comparison, and early exposure cannot reveal full-fleet cost or exercise every infrequent operation.
Signal and evaluation window & Version-specific occupancy, acquisition time, errors, and page latency, compared over nonoverlapping five-minute intervals with a minimum sample.
Control and decision & Increase exposure only when the required sample satisfies both relative and absolute criteria, pause for missing evidence, and restore the approved stable path when an abort condition applies. After restoration, verify routing, resource recovery, and customer outcomes.
Owner and review trigger & The service owner defines the expected improvement and regression criteria, the release owner manages exposure and unresolved pauses, and data owners approve compatibility transitions and the rollback target. Review after any release that is paused or aborted, and before changing the release policy.
:::
